_readme: Starter content for the Coaching Lab: a short performance-foundations layer plus the Advanced Performance Lesson Pack (v2) curriculum. Everything is an unreviewed DRAFT credited to "Mathlete draft" and stays off the live site until reviewed and published in the CMS. Trick lessons leave technique, progressions and corrections marked SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED, which blocks publishing until a specialist supplies them. Loaded by supabase/coaching-seed.sql; run node scripts/build-coaching.mjs after changing this file.

people.name: Mathlete draft
people.bio: Placeholder starter content written to show the lesson structure. Every lesson credited here must be rewritten or reviewed by a qualified coach before it is published.

disciplines.name: MTB Foundations
disciplines.summary: The core movements every other skill is built from.

disciplines.name: Downhill
disciplines.summary: Descending fast and in control on steep, technical gravity trails.

disciplines.name: Jumping & Airtime
disciplines.summary: Leaving the ground on purpose, and coming back down smoothly.

disciplines.name: Dirt Jumping
disciplines.summary: Purpose-built dirt lines: timing, lip awareness and trick progression.

disciplines.name: Slopestyle & Freestyle
disciplines.summary: Style, rotation and expert aerial tricks. Trick technique is taught only with specialist coaching.

disciplines.name: Bike Control & Tricks
disciplines.summary: Moving the bike underneath you: wheel lifts, manuals, hops and pivots.

disciplines.name: Enduro & Trail Riding
disciplines.summary: Riding real trails well, up and down, for a long day.

disciplines.name: Bike Setup & Equipment
disciplines.summary: A bike that fits and is set up well makes every skill easier.

disciplines.name: Race Craft & Analysis
disciplines.summary: Track walks, practice laps, timing, video review, setup testing and race-run execution.

competencies.name: Stability & Balance
competencies.description: Keeping rider and bike stable over the tyres, moving or still, and recovering when balance shifts.

competencies.name: Controls
competencies.description: Precise use of brakes, pedals, grips and dropper: how much, when and how smoothly.

competencies.name: Terrain Awareness
competencies.description: Reading the trail ahead: surfaces, gradients, features and lines, early enough to act on them.

competencies.name: Direction Control
competencies.description: Choosing and holding a line through steering, leaning the bike and looking where you want to go.

competencies.name: Pressure Control
competencies.description: Managing how hard the tyres press into the ground: absorbing, pushing and unweighting the bike.

competencies.name: Timing & Coordination
competencies.description: Linking movements in the right order at the right moment, often in a fraction of a second.

drills.name: Slow Line Race
drills.objective: Build low-speed control by riding a line as slowly as possible.
steps: Mark a straight lane 10-15 m long.
Ride it as slowly as you can without putting a foot down.
Repeat, trying to take longer each time.
Make the lane narrower when it feels easy.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You complete the lane without a foot down
Your time gets longer over attempts
common_errors: Staring at the front wheel
Gripping the bars hard

drills.name: Track Stand Progression
drills.objective: Learn to balance with the bike stopped.
steps: Face a slight uphill so gravity helps you hold position.
Turn the bars a little toward your front foot.
Rock gently against the pedal and brake to stay balanced.
Count how long you can hold it; aim for 5 seconds, then 10.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Practise near a wall or fence you can reach if you lose balance
success: Holds for 5 seconds
Recovers small wobbles without a foot down

drills.name: Ready Position Check
drills.objective: Find and feel a balanced ready position.
steps: Roll slowly on flat ground in the ready position.
Have a friend gently push and pull the bike; stay balanced.
Rise tall, then go low, then return to centre.
Repeat while rolling.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Bike can move under you without you losing balance
Hands stay light on the grips

drills.name: Bike-Body Separation
drills.objective: Move the bike independently of your body.
steps: Roll slowly in the ready position.
Lean the bike left and right underneath you while your body stays upright.
Push the bike forward and draw it back without your chest moving much.
Build to smooth, continuous movement.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Bike leans while your head stays level
Movements are smooth, not jerky

drills.name: Stop Box
drills.objective: Stop smoothly in a target zone using both brakes.
steps: Mark a 2 m box at the end of a straight 20 m lane.
Ride toward it at a steady speed.
Brake smoothly with both brakes to stop inside the box without skidding.
Increase speed gradually as you get consistent.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Stops in the box without skidding
Body stays balanced, heels down
common_errors: Grabbing the brakes
Leaning forward as you stop

drills.name: Brake Before the Turn
drills.objective: Separate braking from turning.
steps: Set a cone 10 m before a wide turn.
Finish all your braking before the cone.
Release the brakes and roll through the turn.
Move the cone closer to the turn as you improve.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Brakes released before turning
Smooth, steady speed through the turn

drills.name: Call the Cone
drills.objective: Practise looking ahead by reacting to signals early.
steps: Ride a loop with a friend standing ahead holding up a coloured card.
Call out the colour as soon as you see it.
Have them change the card at different distances.
Notice how early you can call it when your eyes are up.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You call colours early and consistently
Your riding stays smooth while looking up

drills.name: Walk the Line
drills.objective: Plan a line through a section before riding it.
steps: Pick a short section of easy trail with a few features.
Walk it and choose your entry, path and exit.
Ride it following your plan.
Walk it again and adjust.
drills.environment: Easy trail section with a few roots, rocks or turns
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You can describe your line before riding
You ride the line you planned

drills.name: Cone Slalom
drills.objective: Develop steering and leaning control.
steps: Set 6-8 cones in a line about 3 m apart.
Weave through slowly, looking ahead to the next gap.
Narrow the spacing as it gets easier.
Try leaning the bike more and steering less.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Weaves through without hitting cones
Eyes are on the next gap, not the current cone

drills.name: Figure Eight
drills.objective: Practise turning both ways smoothly.
steps: Mark two cones about 6 m apart.
Ride a figure eight around them.
Shrink the eight over time.
Keep the bike leaning and your eyes leading.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Smooth turns both directions
No foot down

drills.name: Apex Cones
drills.objective: Learn a good corner line.
steps: Set an entry cone wide, an apex cone on the inside and an exit cone wide.
Ride the line through all three.
Finish braking before the entry cone.
Move the apex later as you improve.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Rides wide-tight-wide line
Brakes released before the entry cone

drills.name: Roller Absorb
drills.objective: Learn to absorb and extend over rollers.
steps: Roll over a series of small rollers without pedalling.
Let the bike rise into you on the way up.
Push it down the back side of each roller.
Try to keep your head at the same height.
drills.environment: Gentle rollers on a pump track or trail
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Head stays level
Speed carried without pedalling

drills.name: No-Pedal Pump Laps
drills.objective: Build pumping rhythm.
steps: Start a lap on a pump track with a few pedal strokes.
Try to complete the lap without pedalling.
Count how many rollers you can pump before slowing too much.
Aim to add one roller each session.
drills.environment: Pump track
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Ride in the same direction as other riders
Wait for a clear track before starting
success: Completes more rollers each attempt
Speed maintained without pedalling

drills.name: Lift and Land
drills.objective: Lift and set down the front wheel smoothly.
steps: Roll slowly on level pedals.
Sink down, then shift your hips back to lift the front wheel a few centimetres.
Set it down gently.
Repeat 10 times; then try over a chalk line.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Front wheel lifts without pulling on the bars
Lands smoothly

drills.name: Curb Roll-Up
drills.objective: Use a front-wheel lift on a real feature.
steps: Find a low curb or step (5-10 cm).
Approach slowly in the ready position.
Lift the front wheel onto the step.
Push the bike forward to roll the rear up.
drills.environment: Low curb or step 5-10 cm high
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Front wheel clears the step
Rear rolls up smoothly

drills.name: Rear-Wheel Lift
drills.objective: Learn to lift the rear wheel on its own.
steps: Roll slowly in the ready position.
Shift your weight forward and push the bars forward.
Lift your feet with the pedals to bring the rear up.
Start tiny; aim for a few centimetres.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Keep speed low
Do not use clipless pedals for this drill until consistent
success: Rear wheel lifts without the front coming up
Controlled landing

drills.name: Hop the Line
drills.objective: Link front and rear lifts.
steps: Draw a chalk line or lay a pool noodle on the ground.
Roll toward it slowly.
Lift the front, then the rear, to clear it.
Only raise the obstacle once you clear it every time.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Use soft obstacles that move if hit
Never use rigid obstacles while learning
success: Both wheels clear the line
Front lands first or both together

drills.name: Tabletop Roll-Over
drills.objective: Learn the shape of a jump at low speed.
steps: Find a small tabletop.
Roll over it at low speed with both wheels on the ground.
Practise absorbing the face and extending down the landing.
Gradually add a little speed until the wheels just leave the ground.
drills.environment: Small tabletop jump with a flat deck
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Inspect the jump before riding
Wait for the landing to be clear
Only go bigger once every run is consistent
success: Wheels leave the lip together
Landing on the deck or the top of the landing

drills.name: Small Drop-Off
drills.objective: Practise landings at low height.
steps: Find a 10-20 cm drop with a smooth landing.
Roll off slowly, keeping both wheels level.
Absorb the landing with arms and legs.
Repeat until every landing is smooth.
drills.environment: A curb or ledge 10-20 cm high with a smooth landing
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Check the landing is clear and smooth
Keep speed low
success: Both wheels land together
Rider absorbs and rides away smoothly

drills.name: Find the Balance Point
drills.objective: Feel where the balance point is with brake control.
steps: On grass, roll slowly with a finger on the rear brake.
Lift the front and keep shifting back until it feels like it might loop.
Dab the rear brake to bring the front down.
Repeat, getting closer to the balance point each time.
drills.environment: Flat grass or a smooth car park
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Always cover the rear brake
Practise on grass when learning to loop out
Use flat pedals so you can step off the back
success: Uses the rear brake to recover every time
Holds the front up a little longer each attempt

drills.name: Pressure Test Loop
drills.objective: Find your tyre pressure by testing.
steps: Ride a short loop with a few corners at your starting pressure.
Note how the tyres feel.
Change pressure slightly and ride again.
Keep notes of what felt best for each kind of trail.
drills.environment: A short familiar loop
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You have a written pressure for each trail type
Tyres grip without squirming or bottoming

drills.name: Video review session
drills.objective: Turn footage into one clear focus for your next session.
steps: Collect footage of several attempts at the same feature or section, filmed from the same position.
Watch an expert demonstration of the skill from a similar angle.
Go through the lesson’s “Review your riding” list and note what you see on each attempt, not just the best one.
Write down one thing to work on next session, and what would show it improved.
Share the notes and footage with your coach if you have one.
drills.environment: Off the bike, anywhere with a screen
safety: Film only from safe positions off the riding line, and only with the rider’s agreement (and a guardian’s, for minors)
success: You can name one specific focus and how you’ll know it changed
Notes describe what happened on each attempt, not just the best one
common_errors: Judging the session by one good attempt
Trying to fix everything at once

drills.name: Coach session brief
drills.objective: Prepare for a coach-led session on a high-consequence skill.
steps: Write down the skill and what you want from the session.
Gather evidence of where you are now: recent footage, how consistent your prerequisite skills are, any recent crashes or injuries.
List your questions for the coach.
Check what the facility requires (airbag or foam pit, supervision, protective equipment) and bring it.
Agree with your coach, before riding, what the session will and won’t include and when you’ll stop.
drills.environment: Off the bike, before a coach-led session at a suitable facility
safety: High-consequence skills are practised only with a qualified specialist coach, in a facility built for it
success: The coach has what they need to plan the session
You both agree on the stopping rules before riding
common_errors: Arriving with no evidence of prerequisite consistency
Treating the session as a chance to “just try it”

drills.name: Feature inspection walk
drills.objective: Read a feature or line on foot before riding it.
steps: Walk up the approach, the takeoff or entry, and the landing or exit.
Note the shape: how steep and long the takeoff is, where the landing starts, what the run-out is like.
Check the surface: dry, loose, wet, rutted, damaged lips or landings.
Decide your intent (roll, pump, jump, or skip it) and what speed you’ll build up from.
If anything looks wrong, don’t ride it; report damage to the venue.
equipment: Your eyes, and a coach if possible
drills.environment: On foot at the feature or section, with the line clear of riders
safety: Stand clear of the riding line and landing zones; watch for riders
success: You can describe the takeoff, landing and run-out before riding
You have a clear intent and a starting speed plan
common_errors: Skipping the walk on a familiar feature that has changed
Inspecting the takeoff but not the landing

drills.name: One change at a time
drills.objective: Test a single change on a known section and record what happened.
steps: Pick a short, familiar section you can ride repeatably.
Ride a few baseline runs with the same intent and record them (video, timing or notes).
Change one thing only: a line, a braking marker, a body-position focus, or one setting.
Ride the same number of runs again and record them the same way.
Compare the spread across runs, not just the best one, and write down what changed.
drills.environment: A familiar, low-consequence section you can repeat, with a safe return route
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
Keep intensity below race pace while testing
Stop when tired; fatigue spoils the comparison
success: Only one variable changed between sets
The comparison uses several runs, not one
common_errors: Changing two things and not knowing which mattered
Treating one faster run as proof

drills.name: Consistency set on a known jump
drills.objective: Measure how repeatable your jumping is on a feature you already ride well.
steps: With a coach or experienced rider, choose a familiar jump you ride confidently and comfortably within your ability.
Set a camera in a safe, fixed spot off the landing and line.
Before each attempt, say what you intend: same speed, same shape, same landing spot.
Ride a set of attempts with rest between them.
Review the footage for takeoff timing, flight posture and touchdown point across every attempt.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A familiar, well-maintained jump within your ability, at a venue built for jumping
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
Never increase size or speed during a consistency set
Stop if the landing or lip gets damaged, or you start to tire
success: Your touchdown point and bike angle are similar across attempts
You can explain the attempts that differed
common_errors: Adding speed to “make it better”
Only reviewing the best attempt

drills.name: Range-of-motion runs
drills.objective: Find and widen the range you can move the bike through at speed.
steps: On a smooth, familiar section, ride a few runs deliberately exaggerating bike movement: push it down into every dip, let it rise high over every bump.
Ride the same section again with smaller, well-timed movements.
Move to a slightly rougher section only when the movements feel smooth.
Film a run and compare how much your head moves versus the bike.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: Familiar, low-consequence section of trail or pump track
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: Your head travels more smoothly than the bike
Movements are timed to the terrain, not random
common_errors: Exaggerating so much you lose balance
Going straight to the roughest section

drills.name: Corner entry and exit film session
drills.objective: See what your cornering habit actually is.
steps: Pick two or three corners of different shapes on a familiar section.
Set a camera safely outside the corner where it sees entry and exit.
Ride several runs at a steady, repeatable pace.
Review: where braking ended, where you turned in, front-wheel pressure, and exit line.
Choose one change and test it with the one-change-at-a-time drill.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: Familiar corners on a flow trail, bike park or downhill track
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: You can name your most common cornering habit
Braking ends at the same point across runs
common_errors: Filming from the inside of the turn, in the line
Changing several things after one review

drills.name: Braking-marker runs
drills.objective: Find a braking marker that gives the best exit, and test it.
steps: With a coach, choose a corner on a familiar section and pick a visual marker where braking should end.
Ride several runs aiming to be off the brakes by that marker.
Note exit speed and how the corner felt; film or time if you can.
Move the marker slightly, one change only, and repeat.
Keep the marker that gave the best, most repeatable exit.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A familiar corner with a clear braking zone and safe run-off
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: Braking ends at the marker on most runs
You can explain which marker gave the better exit
common_errors: Moving the marker every run
Braking later until something goes wrong

drills.name: Two-line comparison
drills.objective: Compare two lines through the same section with evidence.
steps: Walk a section and agree two realistic lines with your coach or riding partner.
Ride line A several times at a steady, repeatable pace; film or time it.
Ride line B the same number of times, the same way.
Compare exit speed, smoothness, mistakes and spread, not just the best run.
Note how conditions might change the answer.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A section with two realistic lines and safe run-off
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: You can say which line is faster and which is more repeatable
The comparison uses several runs per line
common_errors: Riding line B faster because you’re warmed up
Deciding after one run

drills.name: Visual reference runs
drills.objective: Set and use visual references at race-like pace.
steps: Walk a section and choose a visual reference for each key point: braking end, apex, exit.
Ride at moderate pace saying (or thinking) each reference as your eyes reach it.
Raise pace gradually while keeping the references early.
Review helmet-camera footage to see whether your eyes reached each reference in time.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A familiar section you can repeat
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: Your eyes reach each reference before you need it
Fewer late corrections on review
common_errors: Raising pace before the references are reliable

drills.name: Whole-section flow runs
drills.objective: Link several features with controlled exits.
steps: Choose three to five consecutive features on a familiar section and mark the decision points.
Ride the section at moderate pace focusing only on exits.
Review footage or timing for the section as a whole, not each feature.
Change one decision point and compare.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A familiar section of linked features
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: Controlled exits from every feature
Section time or flow improves without new mistakes
common_errors: Judging by one feature
Adding pace before the section links

drills.name: Conditions-changed check
drills.objective: Rebuild your plan for a section when the surface changes.
steps: Before riding at pace, walk or ride slowly through each key section.
Note where the surface is wetter, looser or more polished than before.
Move braking zones and adjust lines where grip has changed.
Ride at reduced pace first, then build up only if the section feels predictable.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A familiar section after a change in weather or track condition
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: A changed plan for each key section
No surprises at reduced pace before building up
common_errors: Skipping the check on a familiar trail

drills.name: Track walk and line map
drills.objective: Turn a walk into a plan you can test.
steps: Walk the track during official walking time; stay off the line when riders are present.
For each section, note features, line options, braking zones and risk areas.
Mark questions to answer in practice (which line, which braking marker).
After practice laps, compare with footage and update the map with your coach and mechanic.
drills.environment: On foot at a race or practice venue during walking time
safety: Walk only when allowed, and stay off the line when riders are on track
success: Each section has lines, braking zones and questions marked
The map is updated after practice
common_errors: Treating the walk plan as final

drills.name: Lap and change log
drills.objective: Keep a usable record of practice.
steps: For each run, record date, venue, conditions, tyres and setup, intent, and any change made.
Record total time and section splits if your timing is reliable; note the timing method.
Add one line on what you felt and one on what the video showed.
At the end of the session, write the one conclusion you’re confident in.
drills.environment: Off the bike, during and after practice
safety: Write notes only when stopped and off the track, never while riding
success: Every run has conditions, setup and intent recorded
Conclusions match the evidence
common_errors: Writing conclusions from one run

drills.name: Either-side test
drills.objective: See what one adjustment really does.
steps: Ride your baseline setting on a short, repeatable section and note what the bike does.
Change one setting a little in one direction, within the manufacturer’s range, and ride the same way.
Return to baseline, then change the same setting the same amount in the other direction, and ride again.
Compare the three and keep the one that solved the symptom without creating another.
drills.environment: A short, repeatable test section
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
Stay within the manufacturer’s ranges
Have a qualified technician check anything you’re unsure of
success: You can describe what the change did
Settings recorded for every run
common_errors: Big changes
Testing on different sections

drills.name: Race-run rehearsal
drills.objective: Rehearse your plan and routine before race day.
steps: Write your run plan: lines, braking markers and commitments, from practice evidence.
Do your full warm-up and pre-run routine.
Ride one run at race intent within the plan.
Debrief against the plan and adjust only what the evidence supports.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: Practice runs on a practised track
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: Run follows the plan
Debrief identifies one clear adjustment
common_errors: Trying new lines in the rehearsal

drills.name: Call your intent
drills.objective: Match what you do on a feature to what you meant to do.
steps: With a coach, pick a familiar, low-consequence feature you can ride repeatably.
Before each attempt, say your intent out loud: absorb and stay low, pump, or boost.
Film each attempt from the same safe position.
Review: did the trajectory and exit match the intent?
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A familiar roller or small trail feature chosen with a coach
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: Most attempts match the stated intent
You can explain the ones that didn’t
common_errors: Changing intent mid-feature
Treating getting air as success

drills.name: Full-line transition review
drills.objective: See how each landing sets up the next takeoff.
steps: With a coach, choose a line you can already ride section by section.
Film the full line from a safe position, over several runs.
Review each transition: landing spot, pumps, speed into the next lip.
Pick the weakest transition and work on it in isolation with your coach.
equipment: Protective equipment listed in the lesson
drills.environment: A familiar jump line at a suitable venue
safety: Helmet suited to the terrain (full face for downhill, park and jumps)
Check brakes, tyres and bolts before riding
success: Consistent speed into each lip
Clear identification of the weakest transition
common_errors: Reviewing only the best run

mistakes.name: Eyes on the front wheel
mistakes.description: Looking down at the ground right in front of you.
mistakes.looks_like: Head tilted down, frequent wobbles, late reactions.
mistakes.cause: Nerves or concentrating too hard on the bike instead of the path.
mistakes.correction: Pick a point 5-10 m ahead and keep your eyes there. Your peripheral vision handles what is close.

mistakes.name: Death grip on the bars
mistakes.description: Holding the grips so tightly that the bike can't move under you.
mistakes.looks_like: White knuckles, locked elbows, the whole body moves with every bump.
mistakes.cause: Tension and trying to control the bike through your hands.
mistakes.correction: Hold the grips firmly enough to control them, no more. Let your weight go through your feet.

mistakes.name: Locked arms and legs
mistakes.description: Standing tall and stiff with straight elbows and knees.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider looks upright and rigid, bounced around by small bumps.
mistakes.cause: Nervousness, or not knowing that bent limbs are the goal.
mistakes.correction: Lower your chest and bend your elbows until they point slightly out. Let the bike move under you.

mistakes.name: Hanging off the back
mistakes.description: Pushing the hips far behind the saddle, especially on steeper ground.
mistakes.looks_like: Arms straight, front wheel light and hard to steer.
mistakes.cause: Fear of going over the bars on descents.
mistakes.correction: Stay centred over the pedals relative to gravity. Move back only as much as the slope needs, with your arms still bent.

mistakes.name: Rear brake only
mistakes.description: Using only the rear brake, often from fear of the front.
mistakes.looks_like: Long skid marks, slow stops, rear wheel sliding.
mistakes.cause: Worry that the front brake will throw you over the bars.
mistakes.correction: Practise smooth front braking on flat ground with your heels down. The front brake does most of the stopping when you're braced.

mistakes.name: Braking in the corner
mistakes.description: Grabbing the brakes while already turning.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike stands up and runs wide, or the front tyre slides.
mistakes.cause: Entering too fast and reacting late.
mistakes.correction: Do your braking before the turn, on the straight, so you can release and let the tyres grip through it.

mistakes.name: Target fixation
mistakes.description: Staring at the obstacle you want to avoid.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider rides straight into the rock or tree they were worried about.
mistakes.cause: Your bike tends to go where your eyes go.
mistakes.correction: Look at the gap or line you want to ride, not at the obstacle.

mistakes.name: Leaning with the bike
mistakes.description: Tilting your whole body with the bike like a motorbike racer.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider and bike lean as one; front tyre washes out on loose surfaces.
mistakes.cause: Copying road or motorbike riding, or not separating body and bike.
mistakes.correction: Keep your body more upright and press the bike down underneath you.

mistakes.name: Turning in too early
mistakes.description: Cutting to the inside at the start of the corner.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike runs wide on exit, rider brakes mid-corner or leaves the trail.
mistakes.cause: Eagerness to get round, eyes on the inside edge.
mistakes.correction: Stay wide longer and look for the exit before turning in. Aim for a late apex.

mistakes.name: Pushing on the upslope
mistakes.description: Pushing into the face of the roller instead of the back side.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider slows down on every roller despite working hard.
mistakes.cause: Timing is early, usually from looking at the roller underneath you.
mistakes.correction: Look one roller ahead and wait to push until the wheel crests the top.

mistakes.name: Pulling on the bars
mistakes.description: Yanking the bars up with your arms.
mistakes.looks_like: Bent arms, a short twitchy lift, rider tires quickly.
mistakes.cause: It feels like the obvious way to lift the front.
mistakes.correction: Push down first, then shift your hips back with straight arms. Let your weight do the lifting.

mistakes.name: Lifting both wheels at once
mistakes.description: Pulling up with hands and feet together (a "pull-up" hop).
mistakes.looks_like: Low hop, rear lands first, bike feels heavy.
mistakes.cause: Skipping the front-lift-then-push-forward sequence.
mistakes.correction: Separate the two parts. Practise the front lift and rear lift on their own, then link them slowly.

mistakes.name: Braking on the jump face
mistakes.description: Dragging the brakes as you ride up the takeoff.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike pitches nose-down off the lip, rider comes up short.
mistakes.cause: Doubt about speed, so the brakes come on at the last moment.
mistakes.correction: Set your speed earlier on the approach and keep your fingers off the levers on the face. If in doubt, roll it.

mistakes.name: Nose-diving (bucking)
mistakes.description: The rear of the bike kicks up off the lip.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike pitches nose-down in the air; rider is thrown forward.
mistakes.cause: Riding the lip stiffly or pushing late, so the rear wheel is pushed up hard.
mistakes.correction: Let the bike come up through the lip with soft legs, staying centred.

mistakes.name: Guessing the speed
mistakes.description: Hitting a jump without knowing how fast to go.
mistakes.looks_like: Coming up short onto the deck edge, or overshooting the landing.
mistakes.cause: Not building up speed gradually.
mistakes.correction: Start slow and add a little speed each run, so you always know what the last run felt like.

mistakes.name: Bent arms in the manual
mistakes.description: Holding the manual with bent elbows.
mistakes.looks_like: Front wheel bobs up and down, short manuals, arms tire fast.
mistakes.cause: Using your arms to hold the front up.
mistakes.correction: Straighten your arms and let your hips do the work. Your arms are only connecting you to the bars.

mistakes.name: Rolling a drop too slowly
mistakes.description: Creeping off a drop that's too big to roll.
mistakes.looks_like: Front wheel drops first, rider is pitched forward.
mistakes.cause: Nervousness, braking at the edge.
mistakes.correction: Match speed to the drop, release the brakes before the edge and add a small front lift.

mistakes.name: Tyres pumped too hard
mistakes.description: Running road-bike-like pressures on the trail.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike skips and bounces, tyres slide on roots and rocks.
mistakes.cause: Assuming higher pressure is faster or safer.
mistakes.correction: Lower pressure a little at a time and test. Most trail tyres need far less than the maximum on the sidewall.

mistakes.name: Locked in one position
mistakes.description: Holding one stance all the way down a section.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider looks the same in every frame; the bike and body move together over every bump.
mistakes.cause: A single cue (“stay low”, “stay back”) applied everywhere, or tension at speed.
mistakes.correction: Ride a familiar section focusing only on letting the bike move under you, and compare footage from a fixed angle.

mistakes.name: Losing front-wheel pressure
mistakes.description: The front tyre washes or pushes wide mid-corner.
mistakes.looks_like: Arms straight, hips behind the bottom bracket, front drifting toward the outside.
mistakes.cause: Sinking back for security, or a habit from steeper terrain.
mistakes.correction: Keep a bend in the arms and weight on the front through the turn; practise on a familiar corner at moderate speed.

mistakes.name: Exiting wide
mistakes.description: Running to the outside on the exit and losing the next line.
mistakes.looks_like: The rider brakes again on the exit or misses the next corner’s entry.
mistakes.cause: Early turn-in, late vision, or too much entry speed.
mistakes.correction: Look to the exit before the apex and finish braking earlier.

mistakes.name: Over-braking
mistakes.description: Braking more, or for longer, than the section needs.
mistakes.looks_like: Speed scrubbed well before the corner, then pedalling to recover.
mistakes.cause: Uncertainty about the next section, often from looking too close.
mistakes.correction: Look further ahead to the corner, set a marker, and release when you reach it.

mistakes.name: Braking through rough ground
mistakes.description: Holding the brakes through roots, rocks or braking bumps.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike skips and deflects; the rider gets bounced off line.
mistakes.cause: Braking zones chosen by habit rather than by surface.
mistakes.correction: Move braking to the smoother ground before the rough section and let the bike roll through.

mistakes.name: Shortest-line bias
mistakes.description: Choosing the tightest line because it looks shortest.
mistakes.looks_like: Hard braking, slow exits, and losing time on the following straight.
mistakes.cause: Judging lines by distance instead of exit speed.
mistakes.correction: Compare lines on exit speed with the two-line drill.

mistakes.name: Late vision
mistakes.description: Looking for the next feature only when you’re on top of it.
mistakes.looks_like: Late braking, last-moment line changes, head snapping round in corners.
mistakes.cause: Gaze too close to the bike, often under pressure.
mistakes.correction: Pick exit references during preview and practise reaching them early at moderate pace.

mistakes.name: Relying on a skidding rear wheel
mistakes.description: Using mostly the rear brake on steeps until it locks.
mistakes.looks_like: Long skid marks, the rear sliding sideways, speed not dropping.
mistakes.cause: Fear of the front brake, or habit from flatter ground.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction and practice terrain.

mistakes.name: Riding features in isolation
mistakes.description: Treating each feature as separate.
mistakes.looks_like: Fast through one feature, then braking hard or off line for the next.
mistakes.cause: No plan for the section as a whole.
mistakes.correction: Map the section and ride it focusing only on exits.

mistakes.name: Forcing the dry line
mistakes.description: Riding the same line and braking points as in the dry.
mistakes.looks_like: Slides on wet roots, late braking, off-line exits.
mistakes.cause: Familiarity and not reassessing.
mistakes.correction: Use the conditions check before riding at pace, and test alternative lines.

mistakes.name: Not updating the plan
mistakes.description: Racing the walk plan unchanged after practice.
mistakes.looks_like: Repeated mistakes in the same section; line chosen on foot doesn’t work at speed.
mistakes.cause: Treating the map as the answer rather than a starting point.
mistakes.correction: Debrief after each practice session and revise the map.

mistakes.name: Treating one fast run as proof
mistakes.description: Deciding a change worked because one run was quicker.
mistakes.looks_like: Constantly changing direction based on the latest run.
mistakes.cause: Not accounting for timing error and run-to-run variation.
mistakes.correction: Compare sets of runs and note the timing method’s limits.

mistakes.name: Changing several things at once
mistakes.description: Changing line, setup and technique between runs.
mistakes.looks_like: Can’t say what made the difference.
mistakes.cause: Impatience in limited practice time.
mistakes.correction: Change one thing at a time and record it.

mistakes.name: Fixing technique with setup
mistakes.description: Changing settings to fix a riding or line problem.
mistakes.looks_like: Endless setting changes with no improvement.
mistakes.cause: Not checking footage for technique and line before changing setup.
mistakes.correction: Review video first; only change setup when the symptom is clearly the bike’s behaviour.

mistakes.name: Over-reaching in the race run
mistakes.description: Trying lines or speeds not proven in practice.
mistakes.looks_like: Big mistakes in sections that were fine in practice.
mistakes.cause: Pressure to find time on the day.
mistakes.correction: Race the plan practice proved, and save experiments for practice.

mistakes.name: Casing
mistakes.description: Landing short so the rear wheel hits the deck or knuckle.
mistakes.looks_like: Rear wheel strikes the edge of the landing; harsh, jarring touchdown.
mistakes.cause: Not enough speed, an early push that runs out before the lip, or absorbing the takeoff.
mistakes.correction: Check footage for where the push starts and ends; build speed gradually on a forgiving tabletop with your coach.

mistakes.name: Overshooting
mistakes.description: Landing past the sweet spot, sometimes to flat.
mistakes.looks_like: Long flight, nose-heavy or flat landing, hard impact at the bottom.
mistakes.cause: Too much speed or an unexpectedly poppy lip.
mistakes.correction: Use a repeatable roll-in and build speed in small steps; inspect lips for changes.

mistakes.name: Dead sailor
mistakes.description: Leaving the lip with no movement at all, then riding the bike rigidly through the air.
mistakes.looks_like: Body frozen, bike drifting nose-down or sideways, no adjustment for the landing.
mistakes.cause: Tension, or a jump too big for current comfort.
mistakes.correction: Step back to a smaller familiar jump and focus on a calm, neutral position and looking at the landing.

mistakes.name: Pushing too early
mistakes.description: Spending the push before the lip.
mistakes.looks_like: Legs straight before the wheels leave; bike sinks into the lip and the rear kicks up.
mistakes.cause: Starting the extension at the bottom of the transition.
mistakes.correction: Stay low longer and spread the push across the whole face so it finishes at the lip.

mistakes.name: Boosting by default
mistakes.description: Jumping features that would be faster absorbed.
mistakes.looks_like: Airtime into a corner or rough section, then braking on landing.
mistakes.cause: Habit from the park, or not reading what follows.
mistakes.correction: Practise calling your intent on familiar features and compare exits.

mistakes.name: Nose-heavy landing
mistakes.description: The front wheel lands well before the rear.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider thrown forward, arms collapsing, front pushing on exit.
mistakes.cause: Bike pitched nose-down off the lip, or a steeper landing than the flight path.
mistakes.correction: Check takeoff pitch on video first, then work on matching the bike to the landing on a familiar jump.

mistakes.name: Off-axis landing
mistakes.description: Landing with the bike angled across the direction of travel.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike twists or deflects on touchdown; rider corrects hard on exit.
mistakes.cause: Unplanned sideways movement in the air, or a crooked takeoff.
mistakes.correction: Film from front-on to see where the sideways movement starts; straighten the approach and takeoff.

mistakes.name: Riding a line jump by jump
mistakes.description: Treating each jump separately.
mistakes.looks_like: Pedalling or braking between jumps; inconsistent speed into each lip.
mistakes.cause: No plan for the line’s rhythm.
mistakes.correction: Walk and map the line, then ride it in sections before linking.

mistakes.name: Late recovery
mistakes.description: The bike or body isn’t back in line when the landing arrives.
mistakes.looks_like: Touchdown with the bike crossed up, the rider still out of position, or a scramble on the exit.
mistakes.cause: Possible causes include starting the move late, too little time in the air for the move, or not spotting the landing.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction for this trick and feature.

mistakes.name: Under-rotation
mistakes.description: Not completing the intended rotation before landing.
mistakes.looks_like: Landing short of straight, bike twisting on touchdown.
mistakes.cause: Possible causes include a weak or late initiation, losing the visual reference, or too little airtime for the rotation.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction and bail-out guidance.

mistakes.name: Over-rotation
mistakes.description: Rotating past the intended point.
mistakes.looks_like: Landing past straight, the bike pivoting on touchdown.
mistakes.cause: Possible causes include initiating too hard or not checking the rotation once the landing is spotted.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

mistakes.name: Losing the visual reference
mistakes.description: Losing track of where you are in a rotation.
mistakes.looks_like: Head stays fixed or wanders; landing timing is a guess.
mistakes.cause: Possibly looking for the landing too late or not using visual references through the rotation.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved spotting guidance.

mistakes.name: Off-axis takeoff
mistakes.description: Leaving the lip with the bike already twisting or leaning in an unplanned way.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike drifts sideways or tilts in the air before the move starts.
mistakes.cause: Possibly initiating on the lip rather than at the right moment, or a crooked approach.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

mistakes.name: Late reconnection
mistakes.description: Feet or hands not back on the bike in time.
mistakes.looks_like: Landing with a foot off a pedal or a hand off the bar, or reaching for it on touchdown.
mistakes.cause: Possibly starting the move too late, or holding the position too long.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

mistakes.name: Missed catch
mistakes.description: Not catching the bar or bike cleanly at the end of the rotation.
mistakes.looks_like: Hands miss or fumble; bike lands crooked or the rider lets go.
mistakes.cause: Possibly inconsistent rotation speed or watching the wrong thing.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

mistakes.name: Attempting from a video
mistakes.description: Trying a high-consequence trick because a lesson or video made it look achievable.
mistakes.looks_like: An attempt without a coach, a suitable facility or the prerequisite consistency.
mistakes.cause: Confidence from understanding the trick, which is not the same as being ready to ride it.
mistakes.correction: Stop. Bring your evidence to a qualified specialist coach and practise only where the facility and coach make it appropriate.

mistakes.name: Fish whip
mistakes.description: A whip where the bike flops or kicks sideways without a controlled shape.
mistakes.looks_like: Rear end flicks out and back unevenly; the shape changes from attempt to attempt.
mistakes.cause: Possibly forcing the whip in the air rather than setting it up at the takeoff.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

mistakes.name: Straight takeoff, forced whip
mistakes.description: Leaving the lip straight, then trying to turn the bike sideways in the air.
mistakes.looks_like: Little sideways movement despite lots of effort; the bike stays in line.
mistakes.cause: The whip needs momentum created on the takeoff.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

mistakes.name: Putting a foot down when under-rotated
mistakes.description: Reaching for the ground with a foot to save a short rotation.
mistakes.looks_like: A leg extended toward the landing at touchdown.
mistakes.cause: An instinctive reaction to landing crooked.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved bail-out guidance. Sources warn this risks serious leg injury.

mistakes.name: Uneven leg movement
mistakes.description: Legs moving asymmetrically or jerkily.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike twists or tilts during the trick.
mistakes.cause: Possibly rushed or unbalanced movements.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

mistakes.name: Hose or cable interference
mistakes.description: Brake hoses or cables catching as the bars turn.
mistakes.looks_like: Bars stop short or snag; hoses stretch or kink.
mistakes.cause: A bike not set up for barspins.
mistakes.correction: Stop riding the bike for tricks and have a competent mechanic check routing and compatibility. Never modify brakes yourself.

mistakes.name: Incomplete frame rotation
mistakes.description: The frame doesn’t come all the way round.
mistakes.looks_like: Frame stalls partway; rider lands with feet off or the bike crossed.
mistakes.cause: Possibly an inconsistent initiation.
mistakes.correction: SPECIALIST AUTHORING REQUIRED: coach-approved correction.

skills.name: Balance and Stability
skills.summary: Stay steady over the bike at low speed and when standing still, so every other skill has a stable base.
skills.environment: Flat, smooth, open ground
skills.why_it_matters: Low-speed balance is what lets you hold a line through tight switchbacks, hesitate on a technical move without dabbing, and set up a feature calmly. At speed it shows up as stillness: a rider who doesn’t need their hands to stay upright has more attention for the trail.

skills.name: Body Positioning
skills.summary: The ready position: balanced, relaxed and able to move with the bike over any terrain.
skills.environment: Flat open ground, then gentle trail
skills.why_it_matters: Body position isn’t a pose. Fast riders move constantly, and the range they can move through is what lets them keep grip, absorb impacts and stay balanced as the trail changes. The foundation is a neutral, mobile base you can leave and return to quickly.

skills.name: Braking Fundamentals
skills.summary: Slow down and stop with control, using both brakes and good body position.
skills.environment: Flat open area, then a gentle gravel or dirt slope
skills.why_it_matters: Braking well is a speed skill. Riders who brake hard and early in a straight line, then release, keep their tyres free to grip where it matters. Braking badly, late or mid-corner costs more time than braking a little more.

skills.name: Terrain Awareness
skills.summary: Look ahead, read the trail and choose a line early enough to ride it well.
skills.environment: Easy trail with a mix of surfaces
skills.why_it_matters: Where you look sets how much time you have. At speed, looking further ahead is the difference between reacting and planning, and it’s one of the habits elite coaches keep working on with elite riders.

skills.name: Direction Control
skills.summary: Steer and lean the bike to hold a chosen line, at low and moderate speed.
skills.environment: Flat open area with cones, then easy trail
skills.why_it_matters: Holding a precise line at speed is direction control: leaning the bike under you, looking through the turn and steering only as much as you need to. It underpins every corner and every tight line choice.

skills.name: Cornering Fundamentals
skills.summary: Enter, turn and exit corners smoothly: braking, line, lean and vision working together.
skills.environment: Wide, smooth flat corners, then berms on easy trail
skills.why_it_matters: Corners are where speed is won and lost. Carrying momentum through a turn, instead of braking hard and pedalling back up to speed, is one of the biggest differences between riders of similar fitness.

skills.name: Pressure Control
skills.summary: Push the bike into the ground and let it rise, to absorb bumps and add grip.
skills.environment: Gentle rollers or a pump track, or a grassy slope with small bumps
skills.why_it_matters: Pressure control is the hidden skill behind riders who seem to gain speed without pedalling or braking. Pushing into the trail at the right moment adds grip and speed; letting the bike come up absorbs impacts and makes it light.

skills.name: Pumping
skills.summary: Generate speed without pedalling by pushing into the back of rollers and berms.
skills.environment: Pump track or rollers on a flow trail
skills.why_it_matters: Pumping turns the shape of the trail into speed. On a race track it’s free time; in the park it’s the timing that underpins every jump.

skills.name: Front-Wheel Lifts
skills.summary: Lift the front wheel briefly to clear small obstacles and prepare for manuals and hops.
skills.environment: Flat smooth area, then small curbs or roots
skills.why_it_matters: A controlled front-wheel lift lets you place the front where you want it: onto a ledge, over a root, or into a manual. Advanced riders use small, precise lifts constantly to keep the front tracking.

skills.name: Bunny Hop Foundations
skills.summary: Lift both wheels off the ground to clear obstacles, using a front lift then a rear lift.
skills.environment: Flat smooth area with a soft line or low foam obstacle
skills.learning_commitment: Usually several sessions to link the movements consistently
skills.why_it_matters: A good bunny hop is two linked movements, and the same coordination drives clean jump takeoffs. Riders who pull both wheels up at once hop low and take that habit to the lip.

skills.name: Jumping Fundamentals
skills.summary: Ride small tabletop jumps smoothly: speed, takeoff, a calm flight and a soft landing.
skills.environment: Small, well-built tabletop jumps at a bike park or pump track
skills.learning_commitment: Several sessions on small jumps before moving to bigger ones
skills.why_it_matters: Controlled, repeatable jumping starts with a takeoff that sends the bike level. It’s the basis for jump lines, style and every trick, and the first thing to look at when a rider cases, nose-dives or gets bucked.

skills.name: Landing Fundamentals
skills.summary: Land smoothly after drops and jumps by matching the bike to the slope and absorbing the impact.
skills.environment: Small rollers, then small drops with a downslope landing
skills.why_it_matters: Most airborne crashes happen at touchdown. Matching the bike to the landing and absorbing through it is what lets you ride away fast and into the next feature.

skills.name: Manual Foundations
skills.summary: Ride on the rear wheel without pedalling, balancing with your hips and the rear brake.
skills.environment: Flat, smooth surface such as a car park or grass, away from traffic
skills.learning_commitment: Most riders need many short sessions over several weeks
skills.why_it_matters: Manuals carry speed over rollers, gaps and holes without pumping or jumping, and the balance-point control transfers to drops, step-downs and style.

skills.name: Drops
skills.summary: Ride off small ledges and drops with the right speed and a level bike.
skills.environment: Small, well-built drops with a clean downslope landing
skills.why_it_matters: Drops are everywhere on advanced trails and race tracks. Riding them at the right speed with a level bike, and absorbing into the landing, is the difference between flowing through and getting pitched forward.

skills.name: Bike Setup Fundamentals
skills.summary: Set tyre pressure, suspension sag and controls so the bike fits you and every skill feels easier.
skills.environment: At home or the trailhead, with a pump and shock pump
skills.why_it_matters: Advanced riders can mistake a setup problem for a technique problem, and the reverse. Knowing your baseline tyre pressure, sag and controls is the start of a test process, not a one-off job.

skills.name: Advanced Body Position and Bike/Body Separation
skills.summary: A dynamic position that changes with the terrain, letting the bike move freely beneath you at speed.
skills.environment: Familiar advanced trail or downhill track, then rougher sections
skills.why_it_matters: At race speed the trail moves the bike constantly. Riders who stay fast through rough sections aren’t holding a position; they’re letting the bike move under them while their head and centre of mass travel smoothly. The right position changes with the terrain, the bike and what you want the bike to do next.

skills.name: High-Speed Cornering and Pumping Through Turns
skills.summary: Entry speed, line, pressure, lean and vision as one connected skill, from flat turns to linked berms.
skills.environment: Familiar corners on a flow trail, bike park or downhill track
skills.why_it_matters: Corners decide race times. The difference at the top level is rarely bravery: it’s entry speed set in the right place, a line that keeps the exit open, pressure timed to the shape of the turn and eyes that are already on the exit.

skills.name: Brake to Go Faster: Braking Points and Traction Management
skills.summary: Braking as a tool for traction, speed and line, not just slowing down.
skills.environment: Familiar downhill or enduro sections with corners and braking zones
skills.why_it_matters: Fast riders aren’t the ones who brake least. They brake in the right places, as hard as the grip allows, and release so the tyres can do their next job. Getting that wrong costs time twice: once in the braking zone and again in the corner or rough section that follows.

skills.name: Elite Line Choice: Fastest, Smoothest or Most Repeatable?
skills.summary: Compare lines through the same section on entry speed, exit speed, grip, risk and what comes next.
skills.environment: Advanced trail or downhill sections with more than one line
skills.why_it_matters: The shortest line is often not the fastest, and the fastest line in the dry may be the worst in the wet. Elite riders choose lines by what they give: exit speed, grip, smoothness, risk, and how they set up the next section.

skills.name: Visual Focus and Reading the Trail at Race Speed
skills.summary: Near control points and far planning, and how vision drives decision time, braking and line choice.
skills.environment: Familiar advanced trail or downhill track
skills.why_it_matters: At speed, decisions have to be made before you reach the feature. Riders who look further ahead have more time, choose better lines and brake less, and it’s a habit coaches keep refining even with elite riders.

skills.name: Technical Steeps, Rock Rolls and Front-Brake Confidence
skills.summary: Steepness, surface, run-out and braking options on high-consequence descents, learned on coach-selected terrain.
skills.environment: Coach-selected steep sections and rock rolls with good run-out, progressing gradually
skills.why_it_matters: Steep, technical descents punish hesitation and over-braking. Riders who stay in control use the front brake with skill, keep a mobile position relative to gravity, and know when a line isn’t for them today.

skills.name: Rough Terrain: Roots, Rocks, Braking Bumps and Repeated Impacts
skills.summary: Mobility, line, speed and setup working together through repeated impacts.
skills.environment: Familiar rough sections: root beds, rock gardens, braking bumps
skills.why_it_matters: Rough sections are where the bike gets deflected, tyres lose contact and riders lose time and confidence. The fix is rarely one thing: line, speed, body movement, braking and suspension setup all interact.

skills.name: Linking Features and Maintaining Speed Across a Whole Section
skills.summary: Treat a section as one sequence: each decision sets up the next.
skills.environment: Familiar sections with a mix of corners, compressions, jumps and braking zones
skills.why_it_matters: Races are won across sections, not single features. A corner ridden slightly slower can set up a faster exit through the next three features; a perfect jump that lands you off line costs more than it gained.

skills.name: Wet, Loose and Low-Grip Conditions
skills.summary: Adapting traction, braking, cornering and lines when the surface changes.
skills.environment: Familiar sections in changed conditions, starting well within your ability
skills.why_it_matters: Conditions change what’s fast. Forcing a dry-weather line and braking points onto a wet or loose track is one of the most common ways experienced riders crash. Reading the change and adapting is a race skill.

skills.name: Race Track Walk and Course Intelligence
skills.summary: Map features, lines, braking zones, risk areas and conditions before riding, then adapt the plan after practice.
skills.environment: On foot on a race track or practice venue
skills.why_it_matters: Elite race preparation starts on foot. A good track walk turns a new course into a plan: lines, braking zones, risk areas and questions to answer in practice. A great one gets revised after the first laps.

skills.name: Practice Laps, Section Splits and Video Analysis
skills.summary: A repeatable process: baseline run, review by section, one change at a time.
skills.environment: Race or training venue with repeatable practice laps
skills.why_it_matters: One fast run proves very little. Racers who improve steadily use practice as a process: a baseline, evidence from timing and video, and one change at a time, with notes on conditions, setup and fatigue.

skills.name: Suspension Setup as a Trackside Test Process
skills.summary: Observe, adjust, test, record, with the manufacturer’s guidance and a qualified technician.
skills.environment: A familiar test section, with tools and the manufacturer’s setup guide
skills.why_it_matters: Setup changes can make a big difference or none at all, and riders often blame setup for technique problems and the reverse. A systematic process tells you which, and stops you chasing settings.

skills.name: Race Run Execution, Consistency and Pressure
skills.summary: Turn track knowledge into a run plan, and execute it under pressure.
skills.environment: Race and race-simulation runs on a familiar or practised track
skills.why_it_matters: Race runs reward consistency. The fastest riders on the day are often the ones who executed a realistic plan, not the ones who took the most risk. Knowing what to commit to, and what to leave, is a skill.

skills.name: Jump Performance: Consistency, Shape and Control
skills.summary: From leaving the ground to a controlled, repeatable jump you can shape on purpose.
skills.environment: Familiar, well-built jumps at a bike park or dirt-jump venue
skills.why_it_matters: Getting in the air is easy; doing the same thing every time is the skill. Controlled, repeatable jumping is what makes jump lines flow, what race runs need, and what every style move and trick is built on.

skills.name: Pump, Boost, Absorb and Scrub: Choosing the Right Jump Response
skills.summary: Why expert riders don’t jump every feature, and how they choose what to do with each one.
skills.environment: Familiar, low-consequence trail and pump-track features chosen with a coach
skills.why_it_matters: On a race track, time in the air is often time lost: you can’t brake, steer or pump while flying. Expert riders decide feature by feature whether to pump, boost, absorb or stay low, based on the feature’s shape and what comes next.

skills.name: Landing Mechanics and Flight Control
skills.summary: Alignment, absorption and the landing as the start of the next section.
skills.environment: Familiar, well-built jumps with consistent landings
skills.why_it_matters: A landing isn’t the end of a jump; it’s the start of the next section. Landing aligned and absorbed means you can carry speed and line into whatever comes next, and it’s where most airborne crashes happen.

skills.name: Reading Jump Features and Building a Jump Line
skills.summary: Assess a line as a sequence: approach, takeoff, landing and the speed into the next feature.
skills.environment: Jump lines at a bike park or dirt-jump venue, inspected with a coach
skills.why_it_matters: In a jump line, every landing sets up the next takeoff. A line that works for one rider, bike and setup may not work for another, and the decisions about speed and rhythm are made across the whole line, not jump by jump.

skills.name: Whip: Shape, Timing and Recovery
skills.summary: Moving the bike sideways in the air, under control, and bringing it back in line for landing.
skills.environment: Familiar, well-built jumps at a bike park or dirt-jump venue
skills.why_it_matters: The whip is the foundation of jump style, and one of the clearest tests of jump control: the shape is set up at the takeoff, held in the air and recovered before landing.

skills.name: Tabletop: Style and Bike Rotation
skills.summary: Laying the bike flat to the side in the air and returning it for the landing.
skills.environment: Familiar, well-built jumps at a bike park or dirt-jump venue
skills.why_it_matters: The tabletop is a core style trick and the base for combinations. Done well it shows control of bike rotation and timing in the air.

skills.name: 180: Spin, Fakie and Ride-Away Control
skills.summary: A half rotation in the air and the ride-away that follows.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: The 180 introduces aerial rotation and, depending on the feature, riding away backwards (fakie) or pivoting out. It’s a different skill from a low-speed 180 pivot on the trail, and should not share its progression.

skills.name: 360: Rotation, Spotting and Landing Orientation
skills.summary: A full rotation in the air, from feature choice to landing alignment.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: The 360 is the gateway to rotations in slopestyle. It demands feature selection, clean initiation, visual orientation and landing alignment, and “360” means different things on different features.

skills.name: No-Foot Can and Can-Can Variations
skills.summary: Taking a foot, or both, off the pedals in the air and getting them back for landing.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: Foot-off tricks are style staples and build the air awareness and pedal reacquisition that many later tricks depend on.

skills.name: Tuck No-Hander and Suicide No-Hander
skills.summary: Releasing the bars in the air, in two distinct shapes, and reconnecting before landing.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: No-handers are classic slopestyle tricks that test body-bike stability and controlled release and reconnection. Neither is a beginner trick.

skills.name: Barspin: Rotation, Catch and Bike Setup
skills.summary: Spinning the bars a full turn in the air and catching them, on a bike set up for it.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: The barspin is a signature freestyle trick, and one that needs the bike set up for it: brake hoses and cables have to allow the bars to rotate without compromising braking.

skills.name: Tailwhip: Frame Rotation and Recovery
skills.summary: Rotating the frame around the steering axis while keeping hold of the bars.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: The tailwhip combines several fast, coordinated movements: frame rotation, rider stability, visual tracking and getting the feet back on the pedals. It’s an expert trick with a high cost for mistakes.

skills.name: Superman and Superman Seat Grab
skills.summary: Extending the body back off the bike in the air and returning to it for landing.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: The Superman is a flagship freeride trick. It involves separating from the bike, extending, keeping orientation and returning to the bike before landing.

skills.name: Indian Air
skills.summary: A body-bike separation trick with a distinctive leg and arm shape.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: The Indian Air is a style trick in the Superman family, recognisable by its leg and arm shape, and demanding the same orientation and recovery skills.

skills.name: Backflip: Expert Aerial Rotation
skills.summary: Theory, expert commentary and the coach-and-facility pathway. Not a how-to.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: Backflips are among the highest-consequence tricks in mountain biking. Understanding the physics and what experts say about preparation, takeoff, mid-flip control and landing is valuable; attempting one without a specialist coach and a purpose-built facility is not.

skills.name: Frontflip: Expert Aerial Rotation
skills.summary: How the frontflip differs from a backflip, at a conceptual level. Not a how-to.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: Frontflips demand exceptional precision and carry very high risk. This page explains how the rotation and landing demands differ from a backflip, and points to the specialist route.

skills.name: 360 Off a Drop
skills.summary: Why a 360 off a drop is a different problem from a 360 off a shaped jump.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: Off a drop, the takeoff edge, landing zone and control margins are different from a shaped jump, which changes how the rotation is created and completed.

skills.name: Trick Combinations and Slopestyle Run Composition
skills.summary: Trick families as a skill graph, and planning a run at a strategic level.
skills.environment: Purpose-built training facility with specialist coaching
skills.why_it_matters: Slopestyle runs are judged on the whole run: trick selection, consistency, amplitude, style and flow between features. Training a trick in isolation is different from landing it in a run under pressure.

lessons.title: Balance and Stability Foundations
lessons.introduction: Balance on a bike means keeping your combined centre of mass over a base of support that is only as wide as two tyre contact patches. This lesson refines the low-speed control that underpins trials-style moves, switchbacks and every slow technical section.
objectives: Ride a straight line at walking pace without wobbling
Hold a track stand for a few seconds
Explain why moving the bars and hips keeps you upright

physics.summary: You stay upright by keeping your centre of mass above your base of support: the line between your two tyre contact patches.

blocks.heading: Your base of support is a thin line
blocks.body: Standing on two feet you have a wide base. On a bike, your base is just the line between two contact patches a few centimetres wide. When your centre of mass drifts to one side of that line, gravity creates a torque that tips you further. You correct it by steering the wheels back underneath you or by moving your body.

blocks.heading: Why slow is harder than fast
blocks.body: At speed, small steering inputs move the contact patches under you quickly, so corrections are easy. Spinning wheels add a little stability too, but less than most people think. At walking pace both effects shrink, so your body movements and small bar and brake inputs do more of the balancing.

technique.title: Neutral stance
technique.result: A relaxed, balanced position you can move from in any direction.
technique.movement: Stand on level pedals, knees and elbows soft, eyes up. Weight through your feet, not your hands.
technique.interaction: The bike can move under you without pulling you off balance.
cues: Look where you want to go, not at the front wheel

technique.title: Slow-speed line
technique.result: Ride slowly in a straight line without wobbling.
technique.movement: Keep a little pedal pressure against light rear brake drag. Make small bar movements and let the bike lean slightly under you.
technique.interaction: Pedal against brake gives you fine control of speed.
cues: Eyes on a point well ahead
errors: Looking down at the front wheel

technique.title: Track stand
technique.movement: Turn the bars slightly toward your front foot. Use small forward and back pedal movements against the brake to rock the bike and keep your weight centred.
technique.interaction: Rocking forward and back shifts the contact patch sideways because the wheel is turned.

protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Flat, smooth, open ground
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: You feel tired, frustrated or rushed
The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose
Anything on the bike feels loose or wrong

readiness: You can hold a track stand and ride a narrow slow line without dabbing, repeatedly
lessons.performance_outcome: Hold a line or a standstill with quiet hands and no dab, so balance never limits what you can attempt on slow, technical terrain.
lessons.audience: Riders who already ride advanced terrain, jump or race and want to refine a core movement. Experts revisit foundations too: small gains here show up everywhere else.

Eyes stay up on the exit, not on the front wheel

lessons.title: Body Positioning Foundations
lessons.introduction: The ready position is the centre you move from. This lesson focuses on mobility: how far, how fast and how smoothly you can move the bike underneath you while keeping your weight where the tyres need it.
objectives: Find a balanced ready position on level pedals
Move forward, back, up and down from it while rolling
Explain why your weight should go through your feet

physics.summary: Where your centre of mass sits relative to the wheels decides how much load each tyre carries, which affects grip, braking and how the bike reacts to bumps.

blocks.heading: Centred mass, balanced grip
blocks.body: With your hips roughly over the bottom bracket, weight is shared between the tyres. Move your hips back and the rear tyre carries more; move forward and the front does. On steep ground gravity shifts load toward the front wheel, so you move back a little to stay centred relative to gravity, not relative to the bike.

blocks.heading: Your limbs are suspension
blocks.body: Bent knees and elbows can extend and compress, soaking up bumps the bike's suspension can't. Locked joints pass every hit straight into your body and off-balance you.

technique.title: Level pedals
technique.result: A stable platform for your feet.
technique.movement: Pedals at 3 and 9 o'clock, weight through the balls of your feet, heels slightly dropped.
technique.interaction: Both feet share the load, so the bike stays level under you.

technique.title: Hinge and bend
technique.result: A low, athletic stance with room to move.
technique.movement: Bend at the hips so your chest comes forward, knees and elbows bent and pointing slightly out.
technique.interaction: Bent joints give you range to push and absorb.

technique.title: Move with the bike
technique.result: Stay centred as the terrain changes.
technique.movement: Let the bike move under you: push it into dips, let it come up over bumps, shift back a little on descents.
technique.interaction: Your centre of mass follows a smoother path than the bike.
cues: Centred over the pedals on the slope

protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Flat open ground, then gentle trail
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: You feel tired, frustrated or rushed
The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose
Anything on the bike feels loose or wrong

lessons.performance_outcome: A relaxed, neutral base with enough range to let the bike move freely beneath you in every direction, returning to centre between features.
lessons.audience: Riders who already ride advanced terrain, jump or race and want to refine a core movement. Experts revisit foundations too: small gains here show up everywhere else.

lessons.title: Braking Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: This lesson treats braking as traction management: where your grip is going, how load moves when you slow down, and why the front brake does most of the work when you’re braced for it.
objectives: Stop smoothly using both brakes without skidding
Explain why the front brake provides most stopping power
Brake before a feature or corner, not in it

physics.summary: Braking shifts weight toward the front wheel. That extra load gives the front tyre more grip, which is why it can do more of the stopping, as long as your body is ready for it.

blocks.heading: Load moves forward when you slow down
blocks.body: When you brake, your body wants to keep moving forward. That pushes load onto the front tyre and takes it off the rear. More load on the front means more available grip there, and less at the back, so the rear wheel locks and skids more easily.

blocks.heading: Grip has a limit
blocks.body: A tyre can only provide so much friction. Squeezing the lever harder than the tyre can handle makes it skid, and a skidding tyre grips less than a rolling one. Smooth, progressive braking keeps you under that limit.

technique.title: One-finger braking
technique.result: Full control without losing your grip.
technique.movement: Use one finger on each lever, the rest wrapped round the grip. Set levers so your finger reaches them comfortably.
technique.interaction: Modern brakes are powerful enough that one finger is plenty.

technique.title: Brace for the stop
technique.result: Stay stable as load shifts forward.
technique.movement: Drop your heels and sink your hips back slightly as you brake, arms bent.
technique.interaction: Bracing through your feet stops you being pushed forward over the bars.
cues: Push the bike forward a little

technique.title: Brake before, release through
technique.result: Enter features at the right speed with tyres free to grip.
technique.movement: Do your braking on the straight before a corner or rough section, then ease off through it.
technique.interaction: Rolling tyres grip and track better than braking ones.
