lessons.title: Terrain Awareness Foundations
lessons.introduction: Terrain awareness is scanning ahead, picking out what matters and committing to a plan early enough that your body can execute it. This lesson builds the habit of looking where you want to go, further ahead than feels natural.
objectives: Look further ahead than feels natural
Identify the main line through a section before riding it
Describe how speed changes how far ahead you need to look

physics.summary: Reaction time is roughly constant, so the faster you go, the further you travel before you can respond. Looking further ahead buys time.

blocks.heading: Speed turns time into distance
blocks.body: If it takes you about a second to notice and react to something, at 5 m/s you travel 5 m in that second; at 10 m/s, 10 m. Looking far enough ahead to see features well before you reach them is how you keep up as speed increases.

blocks.heading: Surfaces change your grip
blocks.body: Dry dirt, wet roots, loose gravel and rock all offer different amounts of friction. Spotting a change in surface early lets you brake, straighten up or change line before you're on it.

technique.title: Eyes up
technique.result: See features early enough to act.
technique.movement: Lift your gaze to look down the trail, then glance near only briefly.
technique.interaction: Your peripheral vision tracks what's close.
cues: Look to the next feature, then the one after

technique.title: Pick a line
technique.movement: Before a technical section, choose an entry, a path through and an exit.
technique.interaction: A clear plan reduces hesitation.
cues: Look where you want to go, not at what you want to avoid

lessons.title: Direction Control Foundations
lessons.introduction: At low speed you steer with the bars; as speed rises you increasingly turn by leaning the bike, led by your eyes. This lesson sharpens both and the transition between them.
objectives: Steer a tight cone slalom at low speed
Lean the bike while keeping your body more upright
Explain why the bike leans when it turns

physics.summary: A turning bike needs a sideways force from the tyres toward the inside of the turn. Leaning lines up gravity and that sideways force so you stay balanced.

blocks.heading: Turning needs a sideways push
blocks.body: To follow a curved path, something has to push you toward the centre of the curve. On a bike that's friction between the tyres and the ground. Leaning the bike lets that sideways force and gravity combine through the tyres so you don't tip over.

blocks.heading: Counter-steering
blocks.body: At speed, a brief push on the bar on the inside of the turn starts the bike leaning that way. Most riders do this without noticing. At walking pace you steer the bars directly instead.

technique.title: Eyes lead
technique.movement: Turn your head and look through the turn before you start it.
technique.interaction: Your body and bike tend to follow your eyes.

technique.title: Lean the bike, not the body
technique.movement: Press the inside bar down to lean the bike while your body stays more upright.
technique.interaction: Keeps your weight over the tyre contact patches.
cues: Push the inside grip toward the ground

lessons.title: Cornering Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: This lesson connects the parts of a good corner: speed set before the turn, a line that straightens the corner, the bike leaned and pressed into the ground, and vision leading the way out.
objectives: Brake before the corner and release through it
Choose a wide entry, a late apex and a clean exit
Lean the bike while keeping weight on your outside foot

physics.summary: The faster you go and the tighter the turn, the more sideways grip you need. Berms help by turning some of that sideways force into a push into the ground.

blocks.heading: Speed and radius set the grip you need
blocks.body: The sideways force needed to turn grows with the square of your speed and shrinks as the turn gets wider. Double your speed and you need four times the grip. That's why braking before the turn and using a wider line both help.

blocks.heading: Why berms feel so good
blocks.body: On a banked turn, the ground is tilted toward the inside. Part of the force you need comes from the ground pushing straight up through your tyres, rather than relying only on sideways friction, so you can corner faster with the same grip.

technique.title: Set your speed
technique.result: Arrive at the right speed with brakes off.
technique.movement: Brake on the straight before the turn.
technique.interaction: Tyres need all their grip for turning.

technique.title: Wide in, tight middle, wide out
technique.result: A line that straightens the corner.
technique.movement: Enter wide, turn toward a late apex, then let the bike drift wide on exit.
technique.interaction: A straighter path means less grip needed.
cues: Look for the exit before the apex

technique.title: Outside foot down
technique.movement: On flat turns, drop your outside pedal and press through it while leaning the bike.
technique.interaction: Pushes the tyres into the ground.
cues: Bike leans, chest over the bars
errors: Inside pedal down hitting the ground

lessons.title: Pressure Control Foundations
lessons.introduction: Weighting and unweighting change how hard your tyres press into the ground. This lesson builds timing and range on smooth terrain first, so you can apply it to roots, rocks, compressions and jumps.
objectives: Absorb a small bump by letting the bike come up into your body
Push the bike into a dip to keep tyres in contact
Explain how weighting changes grip

physics.summary: When you push down on the bike, the ground pushes back harder, increasing the normal force and the grip available. When you lift your body, the force on the tyres briefly drops.

blocks.heading: Push down, get more grip
blocks.body: Friction depends on how hard the tyre presses into the ground. By driving your weight down through the pedals at the right moment, you increase that force briefly and gain grip. Rising up does the opposite, making the bike light.

blocks.heading: Absorbing is spreading force over time
blocks.body: Letting the bike come up into you over a bump spreads the impact over a longer time, so the peak force is smaller. Locked limbs mean a short, sharp hit.

technique.title: Absorb
technique.movement: As the front wheel meets a bump, let your arms bend so the bike rises toward you, then your legs as the rear wheel arrives.
technique.interaction: Your body stays at a steadier height.
cues: Let the bike come to you

technique.title: Extend
technique.movement: On the back side of a bump or into a dip, push the bike down and away.
technique.interaction: Tyres stay in contact and gain grip.

lessons.title: Pumping Foundations
lessons.introduction: Pumping is pressure control with rhythm: unweight up the face, push down the back side. This lesson builds it on a pump track so it becomes automatic on trail features.
objectives: Carry speed round a pump track without pedalling
Time your push to the back side of each roller
Explain where the extra speed comes from

physics.summary: Pushing down on a downward slope adds energy. You do work with your legs and arms, and the slope converts that push into forward speed.

blocks.heading: Where the speed comes from
blocks.body: On the back side of a roller, the ground is tilted forward. When you push down into it, part of the ground's push-back points forward, adding speed. Lifting your body on the front side means less of your weight works against you on the way up.

blocks.heading: Rhythm matters
blocks.body: Pumping only adds speed if the push comes on the downslope. Pushing on the upslope slows you down. That's why timing, not strength, is the key.

technique.title: Light on the way up
technique.result: Avoid losing speed on the face.
technique.movement: As you reach a roller, let the bike come up into your body.
technique.interaction: Less force against the upslope.

technique.title: Push the back side
technique.movement: Drive the bike down the back side with arms and legs together.
technique.interaction: Converts your push into forward speed.
cues: Push the bike into the backside

lessons.title: Front-Wheel Lift Foundations
lessons.introduction: This lesson refines the push-then-shift lift so it can be small, quick and placed exactly, rather than a big effortful pull.
objectives: Lift the front wheel a few centimetres on demand
Use a push-then-shift-back movement rather than pulling
Roll the front wheel onto a small step

physics.summary: Moving your hips back puts your centre of mass behind the rear axle, so your weight creates a torque that lifts the front wheel.

blocks.heading: The rear axle is the pivot
blocks.body: When the front lifts, the bike rotates around the rear tyre's contact point. If your centre of mass is in front of that point, gravity pulls the front down; move it behind and gravity helps hold the front up.

technique.title: Compress
technique.movement: From the ready position, push down into the bars and pedals.
technique.interaction: Stores energy in your body and the bike.

technique.title: Shift back
technique.movement: Push your hips back and straighten your arms. The front comes up.
technique.interaction: Centre of mass moves behind the pivot.

lessons.title: Bunny Hop Foundations
lessons.introduction: This lesson refines the hop as front lift then rear lift, so it’s higher, more controllable and transfers to jumping.
objectives: Lift the front wheel with a push and shift back
Lift the rear wheel by pushing the bars forward and bringing the feet up
Link both into a smooth hop over a low line

physics.summary: A hop uses timing to rotate the bike backward, then forward, while your body rises. Your legs provide the upward impulse.

blocks.heading: Two rotations
blocks.body: The front lift rotates the bike nose-up around the rear wheel. Pushing the bars forward then rotates it level again while you rise, lifting the rear. Timing the change between those rotations is the heart of the skill.

blocks.heading: Your body goes up first
blocks.body: Extending your legs moves your body upward. When the bike follows, it's because your hands and feet bring it up with you, not because you jump off it.

technique.title: Front lift
technique.movement: Compress, then shift your hips back to lift the front wheel.
technique.interaction: Bike rotates around the rear wheel.

technique.title: Push forward
technique.result: Level the bike and lift the rear.
technique.movement: As the front rises, extend your legs and push the bars forward and up.
technique.interaction: Bike rotates level while rising.
cues: Push the bars toward the sky in front

technique.title: Absorb the landing
technique.movement: Let your arms and legs bend as both wheels touch down.
technique.interaction: Spreads the landing force.

lessons.title: Jumping Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: This lesson is the foundation for the jump-craft track. It covers the takeoff as a steady push through the whole transition, a calm flight and a soft landing, on tabletops where coming up short is safe.
objectives: Roll a tabletop and land on the deck at low speed
Absorb and extend through the lip to keep the bike level
Explain how speed and lip angle change your flight

physics.summary: Once you leave the lip, gravity is the only big force acting on you, so you follow a curved path (a parabola) set by your speed and the lip angle.

blocks.heading: Speed and lip angle decide where you land
blocks.body: At the lip, your velocity has a forward part and an upward part. Gravity slows the upward part and pulls you back down, but leaves the forward part alone. More speed or a steeper lip means more height and distance. That's why matching speed to the jump is the first skill.

blocks.heading: Why the bike pitches
blocks.body: If the rear wheel is pushed up harder than the front as it leaves the lip, the bike rotates nose-down in the air. Staying centred and letting the bike come up through the lip keeps it level. The simulation leaves this out: it treats you as a single point.

technique.title: Approach
technique.result: Arrive centred, at the right speed.
technique.movement: Ready position, brakes off before the lip, eyes on the landing.
technique.interaction: Predictable takeoff.

technique.title: Takeoff
technique.result: A level bike leaving the lip.
technique.movement: Let the bike come up into you on the face, then extend through the lip with legs and arms together.
technique.interaction: Even push from both wheels keeps the bike level.
cues: Let the lip come to you

technique.title: Flight and landing
technique.result: Calm in the air, soft on landing.
technique.movement: Stay relaxed, match the bike to the landing angle and absorb.
technique.interaction: Spreads the landing force.

lessons.title: Landing Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: This lesson covers landing as the start of the next section: match the angle, absorb, and be back in a ready position for what comes next.
objectives: Land both wheels together or rear slightly first on a downslope
Absorb landings with bent limbs
Explain why downslope landings are softer than flat ones

physics.summary: Landing on a slope that matches your falling path turns the impact into forward speed. Landing to flat stops all your downward speed at once.

blocks.heading: Downslope landings are softer
blocks.body: If the landing slopes in the same direction you're falling, the ground only has to change your direction a little. On flat ground, all your downward speed has to stop at once, so the force is much bigger.

blocks.heading: Absorbing spreads the hit
blocks.body: The same change in momentum over a longer time means a smaller force. Bending your arms and legs on landing stretches out the time.

technique.title: Match the angle
technique.movement: In the air, adjust the bike to match the landing slope.
technique.interaction: Smoothest transition.
cues: Match the bike to the landing

technique.title: Absorb
technique.movement: Let your arms and legs bend as the wheels touch, then return to ready.
technique.interaction: Spreads the force over time.

lessons.title: Manual Foundations
lessons.introduction: A manual is balance on the rear wheel, held with the hips and corrected with the rear brake. This lesson refines distance and control rather than just getting the front up.
objectives: Find the balance point on the rear wheel
Use the rear brake to stop the bike from looping out
Hold a short manual on flat ground

physics.summary: A manual is balance on a single contact point. When your centre of mass is directly above the rear contact patch, there's no torque tipping you forward or back.

blocks.heading: The balance point
blocks.body: Too far forward and gravity brings the front down. Too far back and the bike loops out. The balance point is the narrow zone in between, where your centre of mass sits over the rear contact patch.

blocks.heading: The rear brake is your safety net
blocks.body: Dabbing the rear brake slows the rear wheel, which pitches the bike forward and brings the front down. That's how you recover when you go past the balance point.

technique.title: Brake covered
technique.result: A safety net before you start.
technique.movement: Keep a finger on the rear brake throughout.
technique.interaction: You can always bring the front down.
cues: Finger on the rear brake, always

technique.title: Push then hips back
technique.movement: Compress, then push your hips back and straighten your arms.
technique.interaction: Moves your centre of mass over the rear axle.

technique.title: Hold with your legs
technique.movement: Make small adjustments with your knees and hips; dab the rear brake if you go too far.
technique.interaction: Small movements change torque.
cues: Knees bend to drop the front, extend to raise it

lessons.title: Drop Foundations
lessons.introduction: This lesson covers rolling small drops with a low, neutral position and moving to drops that need speed and a little front lift.
objectives: Roll a small drop with good body position
Lift the front slightly off a drop to land level
Choose a speed that clears the edge to a downslope

physics.summary: Off a drop, your bike follows a curved path. Without enough speed or lift, the front wheel drops first because gravity acts on it as soon as it leaves the edge.

blocks.heading: Why the front drops first
blocks.body: When the front wheel leaves the edge but the rear is still on it, gravity pulls the front down while the rear is supported. The bike rotates nose-down. A small front lift or enough speed means the wheels leave closer together.

technique.title: Approach
technique.movement: Eyes on the landing, brakes off before the edge.
technique.interaction: A predictable departure.

technique.title: Lift and push
technique.result: A level bike in the air.
technique.movement: As the front reaches the edge, give a small front lift and push the bike forward.
technique.interaction: Counters the nose-down rotation.

lessons.title: Bike Setup Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: This lesson sets a sensible baseline from the manufacturer’s guidance and records it, so later changes can be tested one at a time.
objectives: Set tyre pressure for your weight and terrain
Measure and set suspension sag
Position brake levers for one-finger braking

physics.summary: Lower tyre pressure gives a larger contact patch and more grip but less support. Suspension sag lets the wheels follow dips as well as bumps.

blocks.heading: Tyre pressure and grip
blocks.body: A tyre supports your weight with air pressure over its contact patch. Lower the pressure and the patch grows to support the same weight, giving more grip and comfort, but too low and the tyre squirms or the rim hits rocks.

blocks.heading: Why sag matters
blocks.body: Sag is how much the suspension compresses with you sitting or standing on the bike. That reserve lets the wheel extend into holes as well as compress over bumps, keeping the tyre on the ground.

technique.title: Tyre pressure
technique.movement: Start from the manufacturer's suggested range, then adjust a little at a time.
technique.interaction: Balances grip and protection.

technique.title: Set sag
technique.movement: Use the sag markers or an O-ring; adjust air until sag is in the manufacturer's range.
technique.interaction: Wheels can follow terrain.
cues: Follow your fork and shock's guide

technique.title: Lever position
technique.movement: Angle levers so your wrists are straight in the ready position and your finger reaches the lever end.
technique.interaction: Comfort and control.
cues: Straight wrists in the attack position

lessons.title: Advanced Body Position and Bike/Body Separation
lessons.performance_outcome: Your head and centre of mass travel smoothly while the bike moves freely beneath you, with your position changing on purpose for grip, absorption and the next feature.
lessons.audience: Advanced and expert riders on black-diamond and race terrain, downhill and enduro racers, and coaches working with them.
lessons.introduction: This lesson treats position as movement. You’ll look at how far and how quickly you can move the bike under you, how your position changes from compressions to braking bumps to steeps, and why universal cues like “always low” or “always back” fall short.
objectives: Describe how your position should change across compressions, braking zones, roots, berms and steeps
Increase the range you can move the bike through while staying balanced
Use video to spot when you’re locked in one position

physics.summary: Separating bike and body lets the bike follow the ground while your mass, which is most of the system, follows a smoother path. That keeps tyre pressure more even and reduces the forces you have to absorb.

blocks.heading: Your mass doesn’t have to follow the bike
blocks.body:
You make up most of the moving mass. If your body rides up and down every bump with the bike, every impact accelerates all of that mass and the tyres get unloaded and slammed in turn. Letting the bike move underneath you keeps your mass travelling more steadily, so grip stays more even.

On a slope, “centred” means centred relative to gravity, which is why your position relative to the bike changes on steeps.

technique.title: Neutral, not fixed
technique.result: A base you can leave in any direction.
technique.movement: From a relaxed, athletic stance, keep enough bend in arms and legs to extend and compress quickly in either direction.
technique.interaction: Range of motion is what absorbs and pushes.

technique.title: Move with the terrain
technique.result: Grip and stability through changing ground.
technique.movement: Let the bike rise into you on bumps and push it into dips and back sides; shift fore-aft so your weight stays over the tyres relative to gravity on steeps and in compressions.
technique.interaction: Tyre pressure stays more even.
cues: Let the bike come to you
errors: Hanging off the back on steeps

technique.title: Ready for what’s next
technique.result: Every feature sets up the next.
technique.movement: Return toward neutral between features and look ahead so the next movement starts on time.
technique.interaction: Late movements cost grip and speed.
errors: Still recovering from the last feature at the next one

lessons.title: High-Speed Cornering and Pumping Through Turns
lessons.performance_outcome: Corners where speed is set before turn-in, the tyres keep their grip through the turn, and you exit faster, with the same result run after run.
lessons.audience: Advanced and expert riders on black-diamond and race terrain, downhill and enduro racers, and coaches working with them.
lessons.introduction: This lesson compares flat turns, berms, off-cambers and linked corners, and treats entry speed, line, pressure, lean and vision as connected variables. Where the shape of a turn allows, it adds pumping through the corner.
objectives: Explain how a corner’s shape changes your line and pressure
Identify your own cornering habit from video
Pump a berm or compression for exit speed where the shape allows

physics.summary: Grip needed grows with the square of speed and falls as the turn widens. Berms let the ground push you round, so the tyres rely less on sideways grip.

blocks.heading: Why entry speed matters so much
blocks.body: Double your speed and the sideways force needed quadruples. Small amounts of extra entry speed eat a lot of grip, which is why riders who brake a little earlier and release cleanly often exit faster.

blocks.heading: Pressure through a turn
blocks.body: Pressing into the bike as it loads through the bottom of a berm increases the force between tyre and ground, and so the grip available. Letting the bike lighten at the wrong moment, often by sinking back or losing front-wheel pressure, is a common cause of drifting wide.

technique.title: Set speed early
technique.movement: Do your braking in a straight line before the corner. Choose a marker for where braking ends.
technique.interaction: Tyres keep their grip for turning.

technique.title: Line for the exit
technique.result: A line that keeps the exit open.
technique.movement: Choose turn-in and apex for the corner’s shape: late apex on flat turns, the berm’s strongest wall on berms, the inside rut or high line on off-cambers.
technique.interaction: A straighter path needs less grip.
cues: Eyes to the exit before the apex
errors: Turning in early and running wide

technique.title: Pressure and lean
technique.movement: Lean the bike under you and keep weight on the front tyre; press into the bike as it loads through the turn.
technique.interaction: More force into the ground, more grip.

technique.title: Pump the exit
technique.movement: Where the shape allows, push the bike into the back of the berm or the exit compression.
technique.interaction: The slope turns your push into speed.
errors: Pushing too early on the entry

lessons.title: Brake to Go Faster
lessons.performance_outcome: Braking finished in places where grip is good, at a consistent marker, so the bike is free to corner, absorb and pump, and sections are completed faster with more control.
lessons.audience: Advanced and expert riders on black-diamond and race terrain, downhill and enduro racers, and coaches working with them.
lessons.introduction: This lesson reframes braking as traction management. It looks at where the grip is on a section, how braking interacts with cornering and rough ground, and how a coach helps you find and test braking markers. It deliberately avoids universal front-to-rear ratios or fixed braking points: those depend on surface, slope, corner and bike.
objectives: Explain why braking and turning compete for the same grip
Identify where grip is best for braking on a section
Set and test braking markers on a known section

physics.summary: A tyre has a limited grip budget. Braking uses some of it; turning uses some; rough ground reduces it. Spend it on braking where you’re straight and the surface is good.

blocks.heading: One grip budget
blocks.body: Braking and cornering both ask the tyre for force along the ground. Ask for both at once and you reach the limit sooner. That’s why braking in a straight line before a turn, then releasing, often lets you corner faster.

blocks.heading: Where load goes when you brake
blocks.body: Slowing down shifts load onto the front tyre. That extra load is why the front can do most of the stopping when you’re braced for it, and why the rear skids easily.

technique.title: Find the grip
technique.result: Brake where the surface can take it.
technique.movement: On a track walk or slow run, note smooth, straight, grippy patches before corners and rough sections. Those are your braking zones.
technique.interaction: Good surfaces give more braking for less risk.
errors: Braking in braking bumps by default

technique.title: Brake hard, then release
technique.movement: Squeeze progressively to the edge of grip in the zone, then release cleanly before the corner or rough section.
technique.interaction: Rolling tyres grip, steer and absorb better.
errors: Dragging brakes all the way through

technique.title: Markers you can repeat
technique.movement: Choose a visual marker for where braking ends. Test moving it with a coach, one run at a time.
technique.interaction: Repeatable braking gives repeatable corners.
cues: Off the brakes by the marker

lessons.title: Elite Line Choice
lessons.performance_outcome: A deliberate choice between lines through a section, based on evidence from runs and footage, with a line you can ride repeatably.
lessons.audience: Advanced and expert riders on black-diamond and race terrain, downhill and enduro racers, and coaches working with them.
lessons.introduction: This lesson compares multiple lines through the same section, judging each on entry and exit speed, surface, traction, how it interacts with features, risk, and its consequences further down. It tracks line choice separately from confidence and run time.
objectives: Map more than one line through a section
Compare lines on exit speed, grip and repeatability
Explain why a line might suit one rider, bike or condition and not another

physics.summary: Speed carried out of a section matters more than speed in it. A line that’s slower into a corner but straighter on the exit can win the next straight.

blocks.heading: Shorter isn’t always faster
blocks.body: Time is distance divided by average speed. A tighter, shorter line can force more braking and a slower exit, so the longer line with better grip and a faster exit can take less time overall, especially if a straight follows.

technique.title: Map the options
technique.result: Know every line before you choose.
technique.movement: Walk the section and identify each realistic line: inside, outside, high, low, through or around features.
technique.interaction: You can’t choose what you haven’t seen.
errors: Only seeing the line everyone rides

technique.title: Judge the exit
technique.movement: For each line, ask where it puts you for the next feature and how much speed it carries out.
technique.interaction: Exit speed carries down the track.

technique.title: Prove it
technique.movement: Ride each line several times at the same intent, filmed or timed, and compare spread as well as best.
technique.interaction: Feel is unreliable at speed.

lessons.title: Technical Steeps and Rock Rolls
lessons.performance_outcome: Controlled descents of steep, technical terrain with steady speed, rolling tyres and a mobile position, and good decisions about when to ride, walk or decline a line.
lessons.audience: Expert riders and racers descending steep, technical terrain, working with a qualified downhill coach.
lessons.introduction: This lesson analyses steepness, surface, run-out, traction, braking options and body movement on steeps and rock rolls. It discusses front-brake control in context and covers when to dismount or decline. Progression and terrain selection are set by a qualified downhill coach.

physics.summary: On a steep slope gravity shifts your weight forward relative to the bike, and braking shifts it further. Staying centred relative to gravity, and braking without locking either wheel, keeps you in control.

blocks.heading: Centred relative to gravity
blocks.body: On a steep slope, “centred” means your weight line falls between your tyres, which puts your hips further back relative to the bike than on flat ground, with your arms still bent.

blocks.heading: Why the front brake matters on steeps
blocks.body: Braking moves load onto the front tyre, giving it more available grip, while the rear gets lighter and locks easily. That is why skilled, progressive front braking gives more control than relying on a skidding rear wheel. It is a skill, not a rule: surface and gradient decide how much.

technique.title: Assess first
technique.result: Know the whole section before committing.
technique.movement: Walk it: gradient, surface, rollout, any drop at the bottom, and the exit. Decide your speed and braking zones.
technique.interaction: Most mistakes on steeps are decision mistakes.

technique.title: Commit or decline
technique.movement: If the section or conditions are beyond your plan, walk it. That is part of the skill.

technique.interaction: Braking in the rough reduces tracking.

lessons.title: Jump Performance: Consistency, Shape and Control
lessons.performance_outcome: Jumps with the intended trajectory and bike attitude, landing in the same place attempt after attempt, judged by consistency rather than size.
lessons.audience: Riders who already jump tabletops and doubles confidently: park, dirt-jump, freeride and downhill riders, and their coaches.
lessons.introduction: This lesson separates simply leaving the ground from controlling a repeatable jump. It covers jump vocabulary and feature geometry, different performance intents, the rider-bike relationship from approach to landing, and how to analyse consistency across attempts. Casing, overshooting and “dead sailor” jumps are treated as information, not just failures.
objectives: Use jump vocabulary: lip, transition, takeoff, gap, knuckle, landing, step-up, step-down, hip, flyout, tabletop, double

physics.summary: Once you leave the lip, your path is set by your speed and the takeoff angle; gravity does the rest. Consistency comes from repeating the same speed and the same push.

blocks.heading: Trajectory is decided at the lip
blocks.body: In the air you can change your shape but not your path. Speed and takeoff angle at the lip decide where you land, which is why consistent approaches and consistent pushes give consistent landings. Use the demo to see how small speed changes move the touchdown point.

blocks.heading: Pitch comes from the takeoff
blocks.body: If the rear wheel is pushed up harder than the front as it leaves the lip, the bike rotates nose-down. Extending evenly through the takeoff keeps the bike level. The demo treats you as a single point, so it can’t show this.

technique.title: Know the feature
technique.result: A plan before you ride it.
technique.movement: Inspect the takeoff, landing and run-out. Decide your intent and a starting speed well within the jump.
technique.interaction: Intent sets everything else.
errors: Hitting a changed jump on memory

technique.title: Consistent approach
technique.movement: Use the same roll-in point and the same pumps or pedal strokes each time.
technique.interaction: Repeatable speed means repeatable trajectory.

technique.title: Push through the transition
technique.result: A level bike leaving the lip.
technique.movement: Stay low as the takeoff starts, then extend steadily through the whole transition so your legs finish extending as the wheels leave the lip, with arms strong so the front doesn’t drop.
technique.interaction: An even push from both wheels keeps the bike level.
cues: Finish the push at the lip

technique.title: Calm flight, ready landing
technique.movement: Settle into a neutral position, look at the landing, and match the bike to it.
technique.interaction: A calm body gives a predictable bike.

lessons.introduction: This lesson defines a controlled whip and distinguishes it from an uncontrolled sideways bike. Sources agree the whip starts at the takeoff, by building sideways momentum, rather than being forced in the air, and that bringing the bike back in line for landing matters as much as the whip itself. physics.summary: You can’t steer in the air. The sideways movement has to come from momentum you create at the takeoff, and the recovery has to happen before gravity brings you to the landing.

blocks.heading: Why the takeoff matters
blocks.body: Once you leave the lip, nothing outside you can push you sideways. A whip uses momentum created on the takeoff and the way rider and bike move relative to each other. That’s why trying to throw the bike sideways after leaving the lip straight tends not to work.

blocks.heading: Time for the recovery
blocks.body: A whip has to be thrown and brought back within the time you’re in the air. Use the jump demo to see how airtime changes with speed and takeoff: less airtime means less time to recover.

sources.summary: Coach-written article. Favors a steady, powerful push spread across the whole transition over more speed or yanking the bars: stay low on the approach and extend so the legs finish extending at the lip, keep the arms strong so the front doesn’t drop, let the legs do most of the lifting. Recommends filming to see where the push starts relative to the jump shape, and pump-track work for timing. Named errors: pushing too early so the legs run out before the lip, pulling up with the arms, letting the front drop so the rear kicks up, absorbing the takeoff, and relying on speed.

sources.creator: Andy Barlow (Dirt School) with Olly Wilkins

sources.summary: Argues techniques are tools with trade-offs rather than right or wrong, and that some “rules” persist from older bikes and road riding. On flat corners: dropping the outside pedal helps lean the bike and press for grip but can lock you in place and hurt flow through quick linked turns; level pedals help with bumps and pumping but make pressing for grip harder; rider background and height affect which suits. Learning advice: be patient, make sure core skills are solid first, change one thing at a time, and exaggerate technique on easier terrain.

sources.summary: Explains that the whip starts at the takeoff: the rider carves across the transition so there is sideways momentum to use, then moves the bike sideways in the air and brings it back in line with the landing. Taking off straight and trying to turn in the air is the named fault. Suggests flat pedals, wide tabletops and gradual build-up, and notes that landing sideways can damage the rear wheel.

sources.summary: Tabletops are the place to learn because they forgive coming up short; a double removes the middle and with it the margin. Start on tabletops that aren’t too big and build up; only ride a double once you’re confident you’ll clear it; following an experienced rider in is one way to judge speed.
sources.title: The Art of Flight: tabletops and doubles
sources.creator: Olly Wilkins

sources.summary: Pumping and coasting can beat pedalling, especially through tight gaps and off-camber sections where pedal strikes are likely; look for back sides of rocks, roots and downslopes to push into; preload before roots and stay light over them; in linked corners don’t pedal between turns, stay light out of the first and re-weight into the second, then time one pedal stroke on the exit.
